pages.x: By the 1620s the Ming, rulers of China since 1368, were in deep trouble. A cold spell, the Little Ice Age, brought drought and famine, silver from the Americas dried up, and court eunuchs fought officials for power. In the northeast the Manchus, under Nurhaci, went to war in 1618.
Li Zicheng, a postal worker who lost his job when the government cut costs, led an army of starving peasants across the north, promising land and no taxes. In April 1644 his men entered Beijing.

As the rebels broke in, the Chongzhen emperor rang the palace bell to call his ministers. None came. He killed several of his family, then climbed the hill behind the Forbidden City and hanged himself from a tree. He was 33.

The Ming general Wu Sangui held Shanhai Pass, where the Great Wall meets the sea. Caught between the rebels and the Manchus, he opened the gate to the Manchus and joined them. Together they routed Li Zicheng, and a boy emperor of the new Qing dynasty took the throne in Beijing.

The Qing ordered every man to shave his forehead and wear a long braid, the queue, as Manchus did: keep your hair and lose your head. Towns that resisted were destroyed. At Yangzhou in 1645 the killing went on for days, and millions died in the long wars of conquest.

Ming loyalists fought on in the south. The pirate admiral Koxinga, son of a Chinese merchant and a Japanese mother, drove the Dutch out of Taiwan in 1662 and made it a Ming stronghold. His grandson gave it up to the Qing in 1683.

Under the Kangxi emperor, who ruled for 61 years from 1661, the Qing crushed the last revolts and made China bigger and richer than ever. The Manchus would rule China until 1912, as its last imperial dynasty.

The fall of the Ming brought China's last dynasty to power. The Qing ruled for nearly 270 years and doubled the size of China, adding Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang. The queue became a symbol of China until men cut it off in 1911.
